text: Before the group started walking, the leader of the outing took them through the route in detail. Top up your bottles at the spring behind the mountain shelter, he said, because the following water comes only beyond the high pass. The opening stretch follows a track cut with ruts deep enough to twist an ankle without warning. One of the hikers asked why anyone should carry a compass on a waymarked trail. Fog wipes the painted blazes off the rock, he answered, and a marker knocked flat by the weather sends you confidently in the wrong direction. He finished by telling them to cinch the pack straps for the steep climb and slacken them on the descent, to spare the shoulders. They set off while dew still lay across the grass, and everyone repeated the gathering point: the last rocky headland.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)

text: Old trading roads followed the shape of the land far more than the shortest line. A pass that climbed too steeply meant hiring extra draft animals, and that added expense was enough to send the convoys down a neighboring corridor, longer but gentler. Whole settlements grew out of that detour. Where the animals had to recover, someone opened a relay house; a smith set up beside it; before long a market was trading in front of the smithy. Then engineers drove a tunnel beneath the ridge, and the whole pattern ran backward. The convoys took the straight line again, the relay houses stood empty, and the town that owed its wealth to the obstacle faded away once that obstacle disappeared. Travelers crossing those valleys now rarely guess that the quiet around them was bought with a slope.

units: a heavily walked path widens little by little

text: A heavily walked trail grows wider with every single year. Walkers step around the puddles, crush the vegetation along the edges, and what began as a footpath becomes a broad bare strip that channels running water. On spongy heathland, or at the margin of a bog, the process accelerates: saturated ground cannot take the trampling and churns into mud. The people who look after such country have two answers. The first is a timber boardwalk, which lifts every step above the peat and confines the traffic to one fixed width. The second is compacted gravel spread over a filter fabric, so the water drains through the layer instead of carrying the surface away. Either way, plants creep back along the margins by the following season, and the trail finally stops eating into the ground around it.

text: What I had kept in my head was a gentle coastline: a generous beach, low dunes you sank into up to the knee. Returning after years away, I found something entirely different. The sea had eaten into the foot of the cliff, and the wooden stairway down to the sand hung in open air, leading nowhere. A fisherman from the village reckoned two winters of storms had been enough to strip the beach away completely. Where I used to run around as a child, foam was slapping against bare rock. In the end, the surprise outweighed the sadness. The same little bay could pass for a holiday picture one year and a demolition site the next, without a single human hand involved. I left by the upper path, the one running past the cultivated fields, and gave up on a shore that no longer exists anywhere.

units: the text lists the precautions to take before a sea crossing to a nearby island

text: Three things are worth settling before you take a ferry across to a neighboring island. Baggage first: nothing shelters that landing from the wind, and a bag left half open empties itself in seconds, so strap the outside pockets shut and tuck your documents into an inner one. Waiting second: the crossings follow the tide, the departure time posted the day before shifts more often than not, and anyone with sense turns up to board considerably early. Seasickness third: the swell builds the moment you clear the sheltered bay, so stand at the middle of the deck with your eyes fixed on the shoreline instead of sitting inside a closed cabin. Arrival last: count on nothing whatever meeting foot passengers, and expect to walk to the neighboring village with your load on your back.

text: At first light the crews finally cleared the last slide of mud that had blocked the road over the pass. The work had started at snowmelt, when a slab of the embankment tore loose above the hairpin bend. Around the middle of the day a digger climbed the slope to reinforce that embankment, while two teams bolted a steel netting across the cracked rock face. The wind carried the dust out over the moorland, where half wild horses watched the machine and never moved aside. Later in the afternoon an engineer walked the roadway on foot, testing the firmness of the fresh gravel with his heel. The barrier was raised again before nightfall. The first cars took the headland at a crawl, and their headlights drew a trembling line along the ridge, like a vein of fire opened in the rock.

units: a coastal dune builds up in stages you can follow without any instrument

text: Watch a coastal dune closely and you can follow every stage of it without a single instrument. Dry sand, driven by the wind off the water, rolls across the foreshore until it meets something in its way: a scrap of driftwood, a tuft of grass, a stranded plank. The grains pile up in the shelter behind it, a small mound takes shape, and the mound slows the wind in turn, so more sand settles. Roots of creeping grass thread through the fresh layer and bind it, and the hump grows upward instead of scattering. Once the crest stands beyond the reach of the waves, a second dune begins to form seaward of the first, with a damp hollow between them. That hollow carries plants found nowhere else nearby, because fresh water rises close to the surface. Cut a gap through the crest with a boot or a wheel, and the wind pours back in and takes the whole thing apart.

units: the author questions the organized drawing of crowds to places the crowd wears out

text: Should we keep drawing crowds to wild places that crowds wear out? The question makes local officials uneasy, since their revenue rides on visitors, and it splits the residents, who take the congestion and get nothing back. The pattern is familiar enough. A place praised in pictures moving across screens can double its visitor count in one season, though neither its parking nor its paths were built for anything like that. Closing such places is not the answer; it would be unfair. Spreading the load is. A free booking slot thins the arrivals out across the week. A shuttle clears the lines of vehicles off narrow roads. Honest signposting sends people toward the next valley over, just as fine and left alone. And we might stop selling quiet as though the supply had no limit.

text: The lighthouse keeper calls her post a trade of patience, and says it has little in common with the job the man before her did. He lived out on the rock for weeks at a stretch, wound up the wick, greased the mechanism, and wrote the visibility down in a paper log. She watches an automatic lantern from an office on the shore, where screens flag the smallest fault the moment it shows. None of that saddens her. The sea asks for the same watchfulness it always did, she says, and the most reliable gear afloat will quit on the night the swell gets up. As a child she went along with her mother on the runs that resupplied the islands, and she kept a taste for empty horizons. The man before her carried every reef in his head; she finds them by their coordinates, and never trusts that alone.

units: the author recommends a coastal route opened recently in spite of its flaws

text: Honestly, this newly opened coastal route is worth the journey, flaws and all. The line of it first: it hugs the water almost the whole way, swinging between clifftop stretches and drops into coves barely wide enough to stand in, and it keeps you off the long paved sections that ruin so many walks. The waymarking next: clean, steady, no unnecessary forest of signposts, though you do pause and squint on the way into the villages. Then the facilities, and here I will grumble a bit. There is nowhere to sit down, the one water point sits a third of the way along, and the composting toilets the brochure promised exist only in the brochure. What carries it, though, is the feel of the thing: surf working below your boots, birds cutting low across the waves, and nobody ahead of you for an hour.
